title: Gymkhana Dubai Opens: London's Two-Michelin-Star Indian Restaurant Hits DIFC
excerpt: The two-Michelin-starred London institution from JKS Restaurants has opened its first UAE outpost in DIFC's Gate Village, pairing Mayfair signatures with its largest set of location-exclusive dishes yet.
body:
• Gymkhana Dubai opened on September 1, 2026 at Gate Village, Building 7, DIFC, serving dinner daily from 6:30pm to 1am.
  • The London flagship earned its first Michelin star within months of its 2013 debut and a second in 2024, making it one of only four two-star Indian restaurants in the world.
  • Executive Chef Rahul Rana, formerly of Dubai's Michelin-starred vegetarian restaurant avatāra, leads the kitchen; roughly 80 per cent of the menu is Gymkhana's greatest hits, with 20 per cent Dubai exclusives.
  • It lands in one of the world's toughest dining scenes for Indian cuisine — Dubai is home to Trèsind Studio, the first Indian restaurant anywhere to hold three Michelin stars.

Dubai's Gate Village welcomed one of London's most famous dining names on September 1, when Gymkhana opened its first UAE outpost. The two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant from Mayfair, founded by the Sethi siblings of JKS Restaurants, has taken a two-level space with a terrace in DIFC, one of the city's most competitive restaurant districts.

Context & Background

Jyotin, Karam and Sunaina Sethi opened Gymkhana in Mayfair in 2013, naming it for India's historic gymkhana clubs — the elegant social and sporting institutions where high society once gathered to dine, drink and celebrate. The restaurant won its first Michelin star within nine months of opening and, in 2024, became the first Indian restaurant in London to be awarded a second star. Times critic Giles Coren once called it the best restaurant he had ever been to.

The Dubai opening follows a run of international expansion: a Riyadh outpost in 2023, Gymkhana Las Vegas at Aria Resort & Casino in December 2025, and a sister restaurant, Ambassadors Clubhouse, in New York earlier this year. The DIFC space seats up to 137 across two floors plus a terrace, designed by Samuel Hosker of North End Design in collaboration with Karam Sethi. The lower level houses a striking peacock bar, with warm lantern lighting, patterned ceilings and Edwardian-style joinery that nods to colonial-era Indian clubs.

Impact & Analysis

Gymkhana arrives in a city that hardly lacks accomplished Indian cooking. Trèsind Studio became the first Indian restaurant in the world to earn three Michelin stars, while Jamavar has cultivated a loyal local following. Diners in DIFC understand the nuances of Indian cuisine and are increasingly difficult to impress — which makes the Dubai menu strategy, described by the kitchen as roughly 80 per cent Gymkhana DNA and 20 per cent adaptation, a sensible bet.

The greatest hits are all present: Kid Goat Methi Keema & Salli, Tandoori Masala Lamb Chops with Walnut Chutney, Chicken Butter Masala, and a biryani cooked in a pastry case. But Dubai also gets the brand's largest collection of location-exclusive dishes to date, including Imli Black Cod with Peanut Podi, Malvani Sea Bream, Makhmali King Crab & Malai Pyaaz, Wagyu Beef Sukka with Bone Marrow, Jackfruit Ghee Roast and Goat Shank Nihari. A recent review singled out the Malvani Sea Bream — skin-on fish in a coastal gravy balancing sweetness and spice — as one of the most memorable things the critic had eaten in some time. Desserts run from Saffron Pistachio Kulfi Falooda to Rasmalai with Emirati Qishta and a Rasgulla Tiramisu, while the drinks list includes a Clarified Lychee Martini with Himalayan timur pepper.

"Dubai has established itself as one of the world's leading culinary destinations, making it a natural home for Gymkhana's next chapter."

— Pavan Pardasani, Global CEO, JKS Restaurants

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, Gymkhana is a British-Indian success story that turned nostalgia for colonial-era Indian clubs into one of the world's most decorated Indian restaurants — and it now plants that flag in a Gulf city where Indians make up a huge share of the population. Its arrival is also a sign of where Indian fine dining is now being judged: not just in London, but in Dubai, where the competition for the diaspora's dinner reservation has never been fiercer.

What's Next

Gymkhana Dubai is now open nightly, with reservations through gymkhanarestaurants.com/dubai. The early verdict from reviewers is that the restaurant translates its Mayfair identity faithfully while giving Dubai genuine reasons of its own to return. With the Michelin Guide's eyes on the city's Indian dining boom, the DIFC outpost will be one to watch when the next round of stars is announced.
